brief.recommendation: Waiting costs ~$147,234 (596s remaining runtime at $14,822/min revenue at risk) and EXCEEDS the 60s degradation tolerance (BIZ-9). Termination is preferred for this may_interrupt, replayable workload (BIZ-5), but MEMORY vetoes direct termination (mem-5492e343115c302e) because the job restarts instantly unless its scheduler is paused first (auditor lessons). Escalation to the pricing team to coordinate scheduler pause + termination is the only path that respects the veto and the revenue exposure.

audit.report: A batch job (price_sync, pid 17902) held a lock idle-in-transaction for 4 seconds, blocking checkout sessions and degrading success to 19% over 30 seconds with $14,822/min revenue at risk. The Database Guardian proposed terminating the blocker, but memory showed prior terminations failed because the job restarts instantly unless its scheduler is paused first. The Continuity Guardian accepted termination but conditioned it on the pricing team pausing the scheduler before kill and verifying checkout recovery and replay completion. Both guardians agreed the decision required human coordination, so the incident was escalated to the pricing team after 33 seconds with no automated action executed.
audit.root_cause: The price_sync batch job (pid 17902) idled in an open transaction holding a lock that blocked checkout, and its scheduler would instantly restart it on termination unless paused first.
lessons: For workload price_sync (BATCH_REPLAYABLE, may_interrupt): pre-register a runbook step to pause its scheduler via the pricing team before any termination, so the kill is effective and does not instantly re-block checkout.
For workload price_sync: add a lock-timeout or statement-timeout guard so idle-in-transaction holders cannot block checkout for more than a few seconds without auto-abort.
For workload price_sync: instrument the scheduler with a 'pause' API and health-check so the orchestrator can verify the scheduler is paused before issuing a termination.
audit.negotiation_critique: The Database Guardian correctly used memory to veto a naive termination and requested the missing registry, calendar, settlements, and impact data in one round; the Continuity Guardian accepted the trade-off but added necessary scheduler-pause and verification conditions, and both rightly escalated when human coordination was required.
follow_ups: Pricing team: document and test the scheduler pause/disable procedure for price_sync and expose it to the orchestrator.
DB team: deploy a lock_timeout or idle_in_transaction_session_timeout for the checkout path to auto-abort blockers.
Observability: add a real-time 'scheduler paused' signal for price_sync so future negotiations can verify the precondition before termination.
